intro:
These exercises take the chapter's two listings and turn them into a single discipline: decide where each unit of work runs before you write it, then make the queue depth, the cancellation path, and the CPU boundary explicit in the code. The recurring question is not "can Tokio do this" but "which surface does this belong on" — inline on an async worker, on tokio::spawn, or on spawn_blocking — and what the runtime does while that work waits.

The payoff is a service whose capacity is designed rather than discovered. A capacity-one channel makes the producer pace itself; a watch signal raced against accept inside select! gives you a drain instead of a kill; and pushing the only CPU-heavy step behind spawn_blocking keeps the IO workers free to do what they are good at, which is waiting on many things at once. Every solution below is argued in those terms.

exerciseSolutions.title: Place each stage on the right Tokio surface
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Walk the chapter's decision tree once per stage. The tree is short: work that mostly waits stays inline or on tokio::spawn, and work that mostly computes goes to spawn_blocking. The classification follows from whether the stage spends its time parked on an external event or spends it holding the CPU.

Awaiting a TCP read mostly waits. The bytes arrive when the peer and the network deliver them; the task is parked at the await point until the IO driver wakes it. This stays on the async workers — inline in a connection handler, or on tokio::spawn if you want it to run concurrently with other work. It must not go to spawn_blocking, because that would tie up a blocking-pool thread doing nothing but waiting.

Ticking a time::interval also mostly waits, and waits in a specific, cheap way. interval.tick().await registers a deadline with the timer driver and yields; the driver turns the elapsed deadline into a wakeup and feeds the task back to the scheduler. While the interval is idle it consumes no thread at all — it is a registration in the timer wheel, not a background thread and not a busy loop spinning on the clock. That is precisely why a runtime wakeup is the right tool: a dedicated thread would burn an OS thread to sleep, and a busy loop would burn a whole core checking the time.

Summing a batch of u32 values mostly computes. There is no await inside batch.into_iter().sum() — once it starts it runs to completion holding whatever thread it is on. On an IO worker that is a problem: a task that never reaches an await point monopolizes its worker for the entire computation, and the scheduler cannot hand that worker any other ready task in the meantime. So unrelated tasks that are ready to run stall behind a sum that has nothing to do with them. The chapter names putting CPU work on IO workers as the single most common way to make a Tokio service mysteriously slow. The sum belongs on spawn_blocking, which runs it on the dedicated blocking pool and leaves the async workers free.

Reading a filesystem snapshot is blocking work and also belongs on the blocking pool. A synchronous filesystem read can block the calling thread for an unbounded time, and there is no async await point that releases the worker during that block. spawn_blocking isolates it so a slow disk does not freeze an IO worker.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Each stage routed to the surface its waiting-vs-computing profile demands.
criteria: TCP read and interval tick are classified as waiting work kept on the async workers, not as blocking work.
The u32 sum is sent to spawn_blocking as CPU-heavy work, and the filesystem snapshot is sent to the blocking pool as blocking IO.
The answer states that an inline CPU sum monopolizes its IO worker between await points and stalls unrelated ready tasks.
The answer explains that time::interval is a timer-driver wakeup that holds no thread while idle.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the accept loop's select! race
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Each turn of the loop in Example 2 enters a single tokio::select! with two branches: shutdown_rx.changed() and listener.accept(). select! polls both futures and proceeds with whichever resolves first; the other branch's future is dropped for this turn and re-created on the next turn.

When listener.accept() resolves with Ok((stream, _peer)), the accept branch increments accepted and calls tokio::spawn(handle(stream)). Admission stays in the listener loop — the loop's job is to admit connections and count them — while the actual per-connection work runs in a separate spawned task. The match also has an Err(_e) arm that breaks the loop with the current accepted count, covering a listener that has failed.

The shutdown branch fires when shutdown_rx.changed() resolves, and it checks two conditions because changed() can complete for two different reasons. changed.is_err() is true when every watch sender has been dropped: the receiver can never see another update, so the only sensible interpretation is stop. *shutdown_rx.borrow() re-reads the current value because a watch channel can carry values other than the stop sentinel — it was created with watch::channel(false), and a future design might push intermediate values through it. The branch only treats the channel as a stop signal when the sender is gone or the current value is true, so an unrelated update would not falsely trigger shutdown. In this example the sender sends true exactly once, so on that update *shutdown_rx.borrow() is true and the branch breaks.

The server task breaks with accepted — break accepted; is the value of the loop, which becomes the value the async block returns and therefore what server.await.unwrap() yields. The printed count is the number of connections admitted before the stop signal won the race. Because the outer code sends true only after both clients have read their replies, both connections are admitted first, so the count is 2.

Per-connection work is spawned rather than awaited inline so the loop never blocks on a single client. If the loop awaited handle(stream) directly, it could not return to select! to race the next connection against the stop signal until that one client finished. Spawning keeps admission, draining, and the shutdown race independent of how long any one connection takes.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The two select! branches: a stop check that handles both dropped-sender and explicit-stop, and an accept that admits then spawns.
criteria: The accept branch is shown to increment accepted and spawn a handler task, keeping admission in the listener loop.
A changed() error is explained as all senders dropped, and borrow() re-checks because a watch can carry non-stop values.
The loop is shown to break with the accepted count, reflecting connections admitted before the stop signal won.
Spawning the handler is justified as keeping the loop free to race the next connection against the stop signal.

exerciseSolutions.title: Bound the producer with a capacity-one channel
exerciseSolutions.solution:
This rebuilds Example 1's shape directly. Create the channel with mpsc::channel::<Vec<u32>>(1) so its capacity is exactly one buffered item, and move tx into the producer task so the producer owns the sending half. The capacity is the whole point: a bounded mpsc does not error when full — send().await suspends until there is room. With capacity one, the first send buffers the [1,2,3] batch, and the second send([4,5]) cannot complete until the consumer has received the first batch and freed the single slot. The producer paces itself against the consumer rather than racing ahead and buffering without limit.

The consumer drives a time::interval and ticks once per received batch, so consumption is paced on the timer as well as the channel. For each batch, the per-batch sum is offloaded with tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || batch.into_iter().sum::<u32>()) and the JoinHandle is awaited. This keeps the CPU step off the async worker — the worker stays free for the recv().await and the interval.tick().await, which are waiting work.

The recv() loop terminates naturally. When the producer task finishes, tx is dropped, every sender handle is gone, and rx.recv().await returns None, ending the while let loop. The consumer then returns (batches, total). For batches [1,2,3] and [4,5] that is two batches summing to 6 + 9 = 15, so the program prints buffer = 1, batches = 2, total = 15.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A capacity-one mpsc paces the producer; the sum runs on spawn_blocking; the recv loop ends when tx drops.
criteria: The channel is built with capacity 1, so the second send().await blocks until the consumer takes the first batch.
The sum runs inside tokio::task::spawn_blocking and its JoinHandle is awaited, off the async worker.
The recv() loop ends when the producer drops tx, after which the consumer returns (batches, total).
The program prints batches = 2 and total = 15 for [1,2,3] and [4,5].

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a watch-based stop signal to an accept loop
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Create the signal with watch::channel(false), keep shutdown_tx in the outer code, and move shutdown_rx into the server task along with the bound listener. The server task owns admission: each loop turn is a single tokio::select! racing shutdown_rx.changed() against listener.accept().

The accept branch counts the connection and spawns the handler — tokio::spawn(handle(stream)) — so the loop is free to return to the select! immediately and race the next connection against the stop signal instead of blocking on one client. The shutdown branch breaks the loop, and like Example 2 it treats both forms of stop: changed.is_err() means every sender was dropped, and *shutdown_rx.borrow() being true is the explicit stop value. Breaking with break accepted; makes the accepted count the task's return value, recoverable through the JoinHandle.

The outer code does its client work first, then calls shutdown_tx.send(true) exactly once, then awaits the server handle to recover the count. Sending after the clients finish guarantees both connections are admitted before the stop signal can win the race, so the returned count equals the number of connections admitted before shutdown — here, two.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A watch signal raced against accept inside select!; the stop is sent once after clients finish.
criteria: The server task owns the listener and watch receiver, and the loop body is a single tokio::select! over the two branches.
The shutdown branch breaks on a changed() error or a true borrow(), and the accept branch spawns the handler separately.
The outer code sends the stop signal once after its work is done, then awaits the server handle.
The returned accepted count equals the connections admitted before the stop signal won the race.

exerciseSolutions.title: Stop a CPU stage from starving the IO workers
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is that batch.into_iter().sum() runs inline on the async worker. The consumer awaits the next item, then computes the sum with no intervening await, then awaits again. During the sum there is no suspension point, so the future never yields control back to the scheduler. The worker thread is held for the full duration of the computation. Individually each operation looks cheap, which is exactly why the slowdown is mysterious: nothing in the code looks blocking, but a task that never reaches an await point monopolizes its worker until it returns.

This interacts badly with the multithread runtime. The scheduler relies on tasks yielding at await points so it can steal and balance work across the pool. A task stuck in a synchronous loop is not stealable — it cannot be migrated mid-computation, and it is not parked, so the worker it sits on is unavailable to every other ready task. Under load, several such sums on several workers leave the pool with fewer threads able to service waiting IO, and the whole service slows even though no single operation is expensive. The chapter calls putting CPU work on IO workers the single most common way to make a Tokio service mysteriously slow.

The fix moves the sum behind tokio::task::spawn_blocking and awaits the JoinHandle. spawn_blocking runs the closure on the dedicated blocking pool, and the await is a real suspension point: the async worker yields while the blocking pool computes, so it is free to service other ready tasks. The totals are identical because the sum is the same computation, just relocated.

tokio::spawn would not fix this. tokio::spawn schedules another async task onto the same IO worker pool — it does not move the work to a different pool. The CPU sum would still run on an IO worker and still hold that worker between await points; you would have moved the problem, not isolated it. Only spawn_blocking changes the pool the computation runs on.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The sum moves from inline (holds the IO worker) to spawn_blocking (runs on the blocking pool), output unchanged.
criteria: The diagnosis states the inline sum runs on an IO worker with no intervening await, blocking other ready tasks until it finishes.
The fix moves the CPU step to spawn_blocking and awaits its result, keeping the async workers free.
The answer explains tokio::spawn keeps the work on the same IO worker pool and does not isolate the CPU cost.
The refactored consumer computes the same totals as before.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design backpressure and shutdown for an ingress service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Runtime choice: the multithread runtime. The ingress service handles many independent connections, each producing Send jobs that can run on any worker, and the multithread scheduler can spread those across the pool and steal work to keep workers busy when load is uneven. Work-stealing is the concrete benefit: an idle worker pulls ready tasks from a busier worker's queue, so throughput does not collapse just because connections arrived unevenly. The current-thread runtime would be the right choice only for a small, embedded, or deliberately non-Send service where a single executor thread is sufficient and you want to avoid the synchronization a work-stealing scheduler implies — not the case here.

Queue bounds: every internal queue is a bounded mpsc with an explicitly stated capacity. The queue from the accept/ingress stage to the processing stage is bounded so that when the processing stage falls behind, the channel fills and send().await on the producer side suspends. That is backpressure: a full queue pushes back on the upstream producer instead of silently growing. The capacity is a policy — pick it for the latency and memory budget you can tolerate, and state it, rather than discovering the de facto policy later from a memory graph of an unbounded queue. The chapter's framing applies directly: spawning faster than downstream can finish is not throughput, it is queue growth with nicer syntax, so the bound is what makes capacity an explicit design decision.

Shutdown sequence: a watch stop signal raced against accept inside select!. While running, the accept loop's select! races shutdown_rx.changed() against listener.accept(). On a stop signal — either an explicit true or all senders dropped — the loop stops admitting new connections first. It then drains: in-flight connection tasks, which were spawned separately from the listener loop, are allowed to finish before process exit. Stopping admission before draining is what makes shutdown lossless for accepted work — no new connections are taken, but everything already admitted completes. Awaiting the spawned handles (or a join set / a counted wait) before exit is what realizes the drain.

Blocking and CPU stages: the filesystem-snapshot reads and any CPU-heavy processing (the batch sums) move to spawn_blocking, off the IO workers. Keeping admission and connection ownership separate — the listener owns admission, each connection runs as its own spawned task — keeps admission, draining, and metrics easy to reason about. The closing point is the concurrency-control discipline: spawning more tasks is not a substitute for bounding the queue. Faster spawning without a downstream bound just relocates the backlog from a queue you can see into task memory you cannot, so the bound, not the spawn rate, is the real throughput control.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Multithread runtime, bounded queue for backpressure, watch-driven drain, CPU/fs stages on the blocking pool.
criteria: The design chooses the multithread runtime for Send tasks and explains the work-stealing benefit.
Internal queues are bounded so a full queue makes send await and pushes backpressure upstream, with capacity stated as explicit policy.
Shutdown races a watch stop signal against accept in select!, stops admission first, then drains spawned connection tasks before exit.
CPU-heavy and filesystem stages move to the blocking pool, and the design notes that spawning faster than downstream finishes is queue growth, not throughput.

labSolution.explanation:
The lab models Example 1's pipeline in plain std so you can see the coupling without a Tokio runtime. A sync_channel with capacity one is the std analogue of the chapter's mpsc::channel(1): it buffers exactly one item, so the producer's second send blocks until the consumer has received the first batch and freed the slot. Producer and consumer speeds are forced to meet — the producer cannot run ahead and buffer without limit, which is the same backpressure the bounded async channel provides.

The only piece to fill in is cpu_subtotal, which stands in for the chapter's spawn_blocking CPU step. In the async version this sum is pushed onto the blocking pool so it never holds an async worker; here it is simply a function the consumer calls. The body is batch.into_iter().sum(), summing the batch into one subtotal.

The consumer loops with while let Ok(batch) = rx.recv(), accumulating batches and total. The loop ends when the producer thread finishes and drops tx: with every sender gone, recv() returns Err and the while let stops. For [1,2,3] and [4,5] that is two batches summing to 6 + 9 = 15, so the program prints buffer = 1, batches = 2, total = 15.

reviewAnswers.question: What are the four moving parts the #[tokio::main] macro hides, and how do the IO driver and timer driver keep the scheduler from blocking on IO or time?
reviewAnswers.answer: The macro builds and starts a runtime that wraps four parts: the task scheduler (which runs ready futures), the IO driver (an epoll/kqueue/IOCP reactor for network and file readiness), the timer driver (a timer wheel for deadlines), and the worker threads the scheduler runs on. The key is that the scheduler never blocks waiting for IO or for time. Instead, a task that awaits IO or a timer registers interest and yields; the IO driver and timer driver wait on external readiness and turn each event into a wakeup that feeds the now-ready task back to the scheduler. Genuinely blocking work is kept off this path entirely by routing it to the separate blocking pool.

reviewAnswers.question: When should a service use the multithread runtime versus the current-thread runtime, and what does work-stealing buy a Send-task workload?
reviewAnswers.answer: Use the multithread runtime as the default for a service whose tasks are Send, because it schedules those tasks across a pool of worker threads and can run many of them truly in parallel. Use the current-thread runtime when the application is small, embedded, or deliberately built around non-Send state, where a single executor thread is enough and you want to avoid the synchronization a multi-worker scheduler requires. Work-stealing means an idle worker pulls ready tasks from a busier worker's local queue, so the pool stays balanced even when load arrives unevenly — throughput does not collapse just because tasks piled onto one worker.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does a bounded mpsc with an explicit capacity provide backpressure, and what does send().await do when the channel is full?
reviewAnswers.answer: A bounded mpsc can hold only its stated capacity, so once the consumer falls behind and the buffer fills, the channel itself becomes the signal that the producer must slow down. send().await on a full channel does not error and does not drop the message; it suspends the producer task until the consumer receives an item and frees a slot, then completes. That suspension is the backpressure: it paces the producer to the consumer's rate. Choosing the capacity makes the slowdown policy an explicit design decision rather than something you discover later as unbounded memory growth.

reviewAnswers.question: What distinguishes work that belongs on tokio::spawn from work that belongs on spawn_blocking, and what happens when CPU-heavy work runs on an IO worker?
reviewAnswers.answer: Work that mostly waits — network IO, timers, awaiting other futures — belongs inline or on tokio::spawn, because it parks at await points and returns its worker to the scheduler while it waits. Work that mostly computes, or that calls a synchronous blocking API, belongs on spawn_blocking, which runs it on a dedicated blocking pool. tokio::spawn schedules onto the same IO worker pool, so it does not isolate CPU cost. When CPU-heavy work runs on an IO worker, it executes with no intervening await and so monopolizes that worker for the whole computation; the scheduler cannot hand that worker any other ready task, and unrelated tasks stall — the most common way to make a Tokio service mysteriously slow.

reviewAnswers.question: In the graceful-shutdown accept loop, why does the shutdown branch treat both a changed() error and a true watch value as a stop, and why is per-connection work spawned rather than awaited inline?
reviewAnswers.answer: changed() resolves with an error when every watch sender has been dropped, which means the receiver can never see another update — there is nothing left to wait for, so the only sane interpretation is stop. It also resolves normally when the value changes, and because a watch can in principle carry values other than the stop sentinel, the branch re-reads through borrow() and only stops when the current value is true. Per-connection work is spawned rather than awaited inline so the accept loop never blocks on a single client: spawning lets the loop return immediately to its select! and keep racing the next connection against the stop signal, which keeps admission, draining, and metrics independent of how long any one connection takes.
